title: Introduction to Deep Learning
oneLiner: Deep learning stacks many layers of simple processing to learn useful representations straight from data.

what.html:
Deep learning is machine learning with artificial neural networks that have several layers. Each layer transforms its input a little, and the stack of layers extracts progressively higher-level features: edges → shapes → objects, or sounds → syllables → words.

Everyday versionLearning to recognise a friend's handwriting: first you notice strokes, then letters, then whole words. Nobody wrote you rules; you learnt from examples. A deep network does the same, one layer per level of abstraction.

The "deep" refers to that depth of successive representations, usually a network with three or more layers.

why.html:
• Lots of data, much of it unstructured (images, text, audio, video), which hand-crafted features handle poorly.
  • Cheap sensors, storage and computation (GPUs, clusters) make big models practical.
  • Automatic feature learning: the network learns the features instead of an engineer designing them.
  • It scales: with more data, bigger networks keep improving while traditional methods plateau.

how.title: Where deep learning sits
how.html: AI is the science of making machines smart (e.g. a robot that cleans a room). Machine learning is one approach to AI: learning from experience. Neural networks are one family of ML models, and deep learning is the technique of using deep neural networks. Data science overlaps with all of them.

how.title: Layers learn representations
how.html: Each layer re-represents the data so that the next layer's job is easier. A model with no hidden layer can only draw a straight boundary; add layers and the network can untangle curved patterns. The number of layers is the model's depth.

how.title: Why now?
how.html: More labelled data, cheaper computation and storage, and better algorithms came together. Andrew Ng's picture: with small training sets the methods are comparable; as data grows, large neural networks pull ahead.

how.title: What it's used for
how.html: House prices from features (standard network), photo tagging and object detection (convolutional networks), speech recognition and translation (recurrent networks, now Transformers), autonomous driving (hybrid networks combining images, radar and sensors), plus weather forecasting, question answering, finding people in images, and recommendations.

how.title: Every DL problem has four parts
how.html: Data to learn from; a model that transforms inputs into outputs; an objective (loss) function that scores how badly the model is doing; and a learning algorithm (usually gradient descent) that adjusts the model's parameters to reduce the loss.

how.title: Data: examples, features, labels
how.html: A dataset D = {X, t} is a collection of N examples. Each example has d features (bedrooms, location, square feet) and, in supervised learning, a label/target (price). Everything must become numbers. More features means higher dimensionality.

how.title: Model, loss, algorithm
how.html: A model is the computational machinery that turns input into predictions; deep models chain many transformations. The loss is defined so that lower is better. The learning algorithm searches for parameters that minimise the loss: gradient descent.

how.title: From program to trained model
how.html: Instead of writing rules for "does this clip contain the wake word?", collect many labelled clips, start with a program whose behaviour depends on parameters, and train it to the parameters that minimise the loss. All programs you can get by changing the parameters form a family of models; the same family can learn "Alexa" or "Hey Siri".

how.title: Kinds of learning problems
how.html: Supervised: learn from labelled examples (regression: how much?; classification: binary, multi-class, multi-label; recommender systems; sequence learning: tagging, speech recognition, text-to-speech, translation). Unsupervised: only features (clustering, generating synthetic data, density estimation). Reinforcement: an agent acts in an environment over time and learns from rewards.

demo.html: Be the learning algorithm: drag w and b to fit the line through the eight houses and watch the loss (bottom right of the readout). Then press Play to let gradient descent do it. Try a learning rate that's too big (slider far right): the loss can bounce instead of falling.

example.html:
Wake-word detection: the slides' running example of defining inputs (audio snippets), outputs (yes/no), collecting a huge labelled dataset, and training a model family.

Application table: real estate → standard NN; photo tagging and object detection → CNN; speech recognition and translation → RNN; autonomous driving → hybrid NN.

Supplementary In mobile networks, deep models classify traffic types from packet sequences, forecast cell load from time series, and detect antenna faults from drive-test images.

misunderstandings: Deep learning is a different field from machine learning.
It is a subfield of ML that uses deep neural networks.
Deep means the network understands deeply.
It only means many successive layers of representation.
Deep learning always beats traditional ML.
With small or tabular datasets, simpler models are often as good or better.
The loss function is the same as accuracy.
The loss is a differentiable score to minimise; accuracy is a metric you report.
takeaways: Deep learning = ML with multi-layer neural networks that learn successive representations.
AI ⊃ ML ⊃ neural networks ⊃ deep learning.
It thrives on large, unstructured data with cheap computation; scale drives progress.
Every DL problem has data, a model, an objective (loss) function and a learning algorithm (gradient descent).
Problems are supervised (regression, classification, sequences, recommenders), unsupervised or reinforcement learning.
thirty: Deep learning is a branch of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers, each learning a more abstract representation of the data. It sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI. It took off because of huge amounts of unstructured data, cheap computation and storage, and the fact that bigger networks keep improving with more data. Every deep learning problem has four parts: data (examples with features and labels), a model, a loss function that measures how badly the model does, and a learning algorithm such as gradient descent that tunes the parameters. Problems can be supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement learning.

opts: A subfield of ML using multi-layer neural networks
